decks.title: Anterior Eye: slit lamp recap
decks.summary: Prof Naroo's recap of the slit lamp: GOC outcomes, setting up the biomicroscope (with and without a focusing rod), every illumination method with its set-up and uses, coupled vs decoupled viewing, fluorescein assessment, RGP fitting patterns, lid eversion and Van Herick grading.
takeaways: Set-up order matters: clean, table height, focus eyepieces (rod or closed eyelid), IPD, patient position, chinrest.
Conical beam is medium magnification at 45–60° in a darkened room (Tyndall effect).
Indirect, retro-illumination and sclerotic scatter need the observation system decoupled.
Specular reflection is seen through one eyepiece only; reduce the angle for deeper structures.
Tangential illumination (about 70°) is for the iris.
Van Herick (Aston grading): 4 = 1:1 wide open, 3 = 1:½ open, 2 = 1:¼ narrow, 1 = <¼ dangerously narrow.

outline.title: Anterior Eye: slit lamp recap
points: Prof Shehzad Naroo, Professor of Investigative Ophthalmology and Optometry.

outline.title: GOC outcomes
points: O3.1 safe, appropriate ocular examination.
O3.4 analysing visual function to plan management (anterior eye and contact lenses).
O3.5b(iii) decisions on treating and managing ocular abnormalities; O3.5b(iv) recognising when referral is needed, including urgent and emergency.

outline.title: Setting up the biomicroscope
points: Clean headrest and chinrest; adjust table height.
With a focusing rod: focus eyepieces → set IPD → position patient → adjust chinrest.
Without a rod: position patient → adjust chinrest → focus eyepieces → set IPD.

outline.title: Focusing the eyepieces (with rod)
points: Turn each eyepiece anticlockwise to maximum plus.
Put the focusing rod at the shared axis of illumination and observation.
Narrow the slit; turn each eyepiece until the slit is just in focus.

outline.title: Focusing the eyepieces (no rod)
points: Patient in place with eyes closed; rotate the illumination arm.
Against movement → move the slit lamp closer; with movement → move it further away.
No movement → the eyelid is at the shared focus; focus the eyepieces on the slit.

outline.title: Slit lamp techniques
points: Illumination: diffuse, direct, indirect, retro, sclerotic scatter, specular reflection.
Viewing: optic section, conical beam, parallelepiped, Van Herick, fluorescein staining, everted lids.

outline.title: Diffuse illumination
points: Use a diffuser (flip-up, reversed mirror — even a tissue).
Low magnification (typically 6× or 10×), wide beam.
General view of the eye and adnexa.

outline.title: Direct: optic section
points: Thin beam, vary the angle, low to high magnification.
Shows depth: AC depth; localises nerve fibres, blood vessels, infiltrates and cataracts.

outline.title: Direct: parallelepiped
points: Broader beam lights a block of cornea, low to high magnification.
Corneal nerve fibres, punctate keratitis.

outline.title: Direct: conical beam
points: Small circular beam, narrow and short, 45–60°, medium magnification.
Darkened room so the pupil is a dark background (Tyndall effect).
AC inflammatory cells and flare.

outline.title: Indirect illumination
points: As direct, but look to the side of the beam — the direct beam can bleach defects from view.
Decouple to focus the observation system beside the beam.
Epithelial vesicles and erosions, iris pathology and sphincter, limbal vessels, corneal tissue changes.

outline.title: Coupled vs decoupled
points: Photos comparing the two set-ups (coupled: illumination and observation focused together; decoupled: offset).

outline.title: Retro-illumination
points: Light reflected from the iris or fundus back-lights the cornea.
Moderately wide beam, decoupled, medium to high magnification.
Microcysts (appear reversed), vacuoles, lens opacities, CL deposits, vascularisation.

outline.title: Specular reflection
points: Angle of incidence = angle of observation; the tear film acts as a mirror (Purkinje image).
Medium to high magnification; focus on the area, then swing the beam until the reflection appears.
Visible through one eyepiece only; reduce the angle for deeper structures.
Tear film debris and flow, endothelium, crystalline lens 'orange peel'.

outline.title: Sclerotic scatter
points: 1–1.5 mm slit on the limbus; total internal reflection through the cornea.
Observation decoupled and focused on the cornea, low magnification; halo of light in a darkened room.
Corneal scars, oedema and foreign bodies.

outline.title: Tangential illumination
points: Illumination and observation almost at right angles (about 70°).
Low to medium magnification, wide beam.
Iris freckles, tumours, general integrity of cornea and iris.

outline.title: Fluorescein assessment
points: Broad beam, blue light with a yellow filter.
Conjunctiva, cornea and TBUT.
Adding the yellow (Wratten) filter makes differences in tear thickness much easier to see.

outline.title: RGP fitting patterns
points: Example fluorescein patterns for RGP lenses (see the RGP fitting topic).

outline.title: Lid eversion
points: Prepare the slit lamp first; cotton bud or finger.
Push lashes apart, hold the upper lashes and pull down, bud at the top of the tarsal plate.
Down-and-round motion; afterwards the patient blinks to straighten the lid.
Look with white light and blue light.

outline.title: Van Herick technique
points: Low magnification optic section, about 60° between illumination and observation (straight ahead).
Compare corneal width with AC depth.
Grade 4: 1:1 wide open; grade 3: 1:½ open; grade 2: 1:¼ narrow; grade 1: <¼ dangerously narrow.

decks.title: CLB Lecture 1: Introduction, history and symptoms
decks.file: Mgmt_CLB_01_CL Introduction History and Symptoms_DD - no vioceover - Tagged.pdf
decks.summary: Dr Dutta's first CLB lecture: the GOC learning outcomes and the CLB plan for years 1–3, why people choose contact lenses, the history of contact lenses, what modern CL practice covers, taking a CL history and symptoms (including medication and contraindications), pre-fitting counselling, and baseline measurements (HVID and pupil size). Ends with the week 1 practical: history, symptoms and baseline measurements.
takeaways: CLB GOC LOs: fit soft contact lenses (LO 5.21) and manage the anterior eye health of CL wearers (LO 5.22).
Year 2 covers history and symptoms, corneal shape, rigid lenses, materials, soft lenses, dry eye, complications and legal aspects.
History = preferences, lifestyle, health, refractive state; symptoms with SOCRATES.
Medication can reduce tears and blink rate; soft lenses absorb topical drops and preservatives.
HVID 10–14 mm (average 11.7 mm); measure pupils in room and dim light.

outline.title: Introduction, history and symptoms
points: Theme: Contact Lenses and Biomedical Devices (CLB), Management pillar. Dr Debarun Dutta.

outline.title: GOC learning outcomes and theme objectives
points: Fit soft contact lenses (LO 5.21); manage anterior eye health of CL wearers (LO 5.22).
Take a history and symptoms; assess the anterior eye (slit lamp, keratometry, dyes).
Fit and assess soft and rigid lenses; prescribe care systems and verify parameters; carry out fittings, aftercares and collections.

outline.title: CLB across the three years
points: Year 1: what a CL is, optical differences, accommodation, prismatic effects, magnification.
Year 2: history and symptoms, corneal shape, rigid lenses, materials, soft lenses, dry eye, complications, legal aspects.
Year 3: myopia management, ortho-K and scleral lenses.

outline.title: Recommended texts and lecturer
points: Phillips and Speedwell (Contact Lenses, 6th ed.), Andersen et al., Hom, Franklin (Eye Essentials).
Dr Dutta: BCLA trustee and academic chair, Fellow of BCLA, AAO, IACLE and HEA.

outline.title: CLB plan for the year
points: Tuesday practicals with a pre-recorded lecture to study first: wk 1 introduction, history and symptoms; wk 2 slit lamp biomicroscope and techniques; wk 3 keratometry and topography; wk 5 RGP design and fitting; wk 6 recording and grading; wk 12 soft lens materials, manufacture and selection.
Tuesday 12 noon lectures include slit lamp revision, RGP design and fit, and soft lens design and fit (compulsory).

outline.title: How to study CLB
points: Study the lectures on Blackboard before the seminar, attend the compulsory seminars and practicals, bring questions, then sit the practical exam.

outline.title: Learning outcomes for this lecture
points: CL practice in the UK and globally; why fit CLs; history and symptoms; key baseline measurements. (Acknowledges Prof James Wolffsohn.)

outline.title: Why contact lenses?
points: More natural vision; no frames slipping or marking; better appearance and magnification (especially for myopes); wider field.
Optics stay aligned with the eye; no fogging; fewer rain and perspiration problems.
Better for anisometropia and irregular astigmatism; good for sport, goggles, cameras and microscopes.
UV protection, cosmetic benefits and myopia control.

outline.title: History of contact lenses
points: Early ideas (Celsus, Da Vinci, Descartes 1637, de la Hire 1685) don't really describe CLs.
Thomas Young (1801) and John Herschel (1827) deserve more credit — Herschel suggested a jelly-filled capsule or a corneal mould for irregular corneas.
Fick (moulded lenses), Kalt (lenses change corneal shape), Müller (−14 D, corrected himself, ~30 min wear), Zeiss (lathe-cut lenses, first trial sets).

outline.title: History of CL (timeline images)
points: Image-only slides — see the original deck.

outline.title: CL practice today
points: Optical correction, myopia control, therapeutic/medical, aesthetic, specialist (drug delivery, scleral lenses).
Increasing silicone hydrogel wear.
Spherical/toric, single vision/multifocal; GP corneal or scleral; soft hydrogel or silicone hydrogel; daily disposable, planned replacement, reusable; ortho-K.

outline.title: History taking
points: Patient preferences: reason for CLs, current lens/modality/brand, years of wear, hours per day, care solution, quality-of-life benefits.
Lifestyle: age, recreation, occupation/hobbies, home and work environment, digital devices.
Health: general health and medicines, ocular health/surgery/medicines, family history, allergies.
Refractive state: non-astigmatic, astigmatic, presbyopic, paediatric/myopia.

outline.title: Symptoms (SOCRATES)
points: Site, onset, character (flare/glare, blur; burning, gritty, itchy, watery, tired), timing, exacerbating/relieving factors (including with CLs), severity.

outline.title: Conditions to look out for
points: Allergy/hay fever, diabetes, systemic inflammatory disease (e.g. sarcoidosis), thyroid eye disease, skin conditions linked to blepharitis, previous eye surgery — onset, type, control, family history.

outline.title: Medication and contact lens wear
points: Systemic drugs can depress blinking, reduce tear volume and cause dryness, irritation, blur or intolerance (e.g. antihistamines, antidepressants, diuretics, tranquillisers, muscle relaxants, alcohol).
Some can increase corneal sensitivity or cause corneal oedema.
Topical drugs and preservatives can be absorbed and retained by lenses, especially hydrogels.

outline.title: Contraindications
points: Low refractive error, horizontal prism, infection/inflammation, recurrent corneal erosion, diabetes, sinus and allergy problems, sensitive or dry eyes/poor blinking, acne rosacea/seborrhoeic conditions, adverse environments.

outline.title: (Image-only slide)
points: See the original deck.

outline.title: Prior to fitting
points: Counsel and document: lens type, modality, care regimen, risks, time to full-time wear, possible visual compromise/discomfort, what to do in an emergency, costs.

outline.title: Baseline measurements
points: HVID, pupil diameter (room and dim light), K readings/topography, corneal shape/scleral dimensions if needed.
HVID methods: topographer, autorefractor, slit lamp reticule, aberrometer, PD ruler; 10–14 mm, average 11.7 mm.
Pupils with a ruler (or Burton lamp): room (photopic) and dim (scotopic). VPA is rarely used now.

outline.title: Today's clinic (week 1 practical)
points: Why wear contact lenses — who to talk to about the benefits.
Hygiene: wash hands well and dry them before handling lenses.

Record history and symptoms on the record card: reason for wear and modality, previous CL wear, ocular history, general health and meds (diabetes, glaucoma, hypertension, dry eyes, allergies), family history.
Baseline measures: what to measure and how.

outline.title: Summary
points: CL practice in the UK and globally, history of CLs, why fit CLs and contraindications, history and symptoms, baseline measurements (HVID and pupil size).
